entries.english: Spellings: Wolechingen 1221, Wollechingen 1239, Wollichingen 1245, Wulchingen 1387, Welchingen 1421. Literature: Ottmar F. H. Schönhuth, Boxberg and the Schüpfergrund, (see above) p. 32 ff., Bauer, Journal for the Wirttemberg Franconia 1868, p. 106 ff., C W F. L. Stocker, Chronicle of Boxberg (see above) p. 44 ff. A Siboto de Wolechingen appears with Bertolt de Mergentheim, both Templars, as witnesses in a Bronnbach document from 1221; the place is mentioned as belonging to the Lordship of Boxberg in documents from 1239 (contract between Gotfried von Hohenlohe and Konrad von Krutheim) and 1245 (bequest of Kraft von Boxberg) (cf. Boxberg). In Kraft's donation to the Knights Hospitaller in Würzburg from 1192, some unspecified properties probably refer to Wölchingen; in 1239, the Knights Hospitaller owned a farm there, which was subject to tithes in Würzburg. Their own settlement, a house, is first documented in 1249 (Konrad de Bvechel, provisor domus in Wollechingen), and a commandery in 1284 (frater commendator domus S. Johannis in Wollechingen). In 1313, it was moved to Boxberg Castle (donated to the Order by the last of the Boxberg family, Konrad). In 1381, Wölchingen and Boxberg passed to the Rosenberg family, and in 1561 to the Electorate of the Palatinate (Oberamt Boxberg); from 1803 to 1806, it belonged to Leiningen. (E.) During railway construction in August 1866, a Frankish grave covered with limestone slabs was discovered directly north of the cemetery. In it, next to the skeleton, lay an iron spearhead and colorful decorative beads made of glass and clay. Upon further investigation, it would likely remain the only one found, but would prove to belong to an entire cemetery. (W.) The church. Nothing is known for sure about the origin of the Romanesque parish church, located on the north side of the lovely Schüpfergrund above the village. Bauer considers it unlikely that the Knights of St. John built the church, as they only owned a commandery in Wölchingen in 1249, and the architectural style indicates an earlier date. In his opinion, however, "the respected lords of Boxberg" could well have been the founders of this building. This is contradicted by the fact that the Boxbergs never erected similarly sumptuous buildings either in their residence above or in Wanshofen, located at the foot of the castle. Furthermore, the Knights of St. John had owned large estates near Boxberg and Schweigern even earlier, namely since 1192, although a farm in Wölchingen is only documented in 1239. Nevertheless, it is much more likely to attribute the construction of this church, which can be seen from afar as a symbol of their power and which virtually dominates the Schüpfergrund, to the rich members of the order, who were well versed in architecture and art, than to the minor dynasts of Boxberg. Frater Konrad sacerdos, mentioned in 1249 in Wölchingen, was certainly also appointed by the Order, so the parish must have been founded by the Order a generation or two earlier. In the liber Synodalis Wirceburgensis, the parish (Chapter Mergentheim), Frühmüsse B. M. V. and the vicarage of St. Johannis in Wölchingen are mentioned for the year 1452. Under the patronage of the von Rosenbergs in the 16th century, i. In 1558, the Reformation was introduced here as well, and confirmed by the Peace of Westphalia. Now the Protestant parish church for Boxberg and Wölchingen. The construction records of the Grand General State Archives on our church begin in 1663, but essentially contain only information of little relevance to the building's history, concerning repairs to the venerable building, which had apparently been badly damaged during the preceding war years. Regarding the condition of the building at the time when the Protestant building authority began its most recent repairs, the construction officer, Baurat Behaghel, in Heidelberg, wrote the following: "The existing structure at that time was not suitable for systematic graphic recording, as it presented a far from pleasing image, and moreover, the original form of the building was almost obscured from view by a conglomerate of the most primitive structural makeshift structures. These makeshift structures, which, however, survived for centuries, consisted of superstructures above the only fragmentary main cornice, which, judging by their overall nature, had probably served defensive purposes since its destruction during the Peasants' War, and were composed in detail of fragments of the former tower and gable superstructures, or even of clay timber framing. The old roof truss was poorly constructed from thin, not even square-jointed logs and had been patched up many times over the past few centuries. The bells, which hardly dated back to the previous century, had been hung on the south side of the granary in an ordinary oak trestle frame as a bell cage. The interior of the church looked downright desolate; it was completely built over with colorful, marbled, randomly placed wooden galleries, to which numerous steps led. It had been so diminished with paint and crude, rustic paintings from the end of the previous century that the forms of the capitals were barely recognizable, and the entire church gave the impression of a large junk room. The walls of the north side, which were embedded at a height of about 3 meters in the muddy soil of the old cemetery at the back, were covered with dense green lichen along the entire length of the church, almost up to the level of the vaults, and were so wet that even to this day, the traces of this have not completely disappeared. The crypt was also covered with mud up to the height of the windowsills. Before the restoration, the vaults, made of tuff, were partly in very poor condition, as their plaster was almost completely destroyed due to the hygroscopic properties of the material. As far as the restoration of the church was concerned, the first step was to thoroughly clear and dry the area, along with extensive drainage. Then, all superstructures above the main cornice had to be removed, the previous gables had to be restored, and a crossing tower had to be constructed. After that, the entire interior, after removing all obstructive fixtures, had to be exposed and restored to its original form. In addition to the unsuccessful searches for possible remains of the foundations of a particular bell tower, the examination of the crossing pillars, whose foundations exhibit a quite unusual depth and thickness, as well as individual remains of wall supports at the relevant locations in the attic, all of which supported the earlier existence of a crossing tower. Further evidence came from the various debris found in the superstructure, which, after eliminating the pieces undoubtedly suitable for the cornices, gable ends, and the like, made their former use in a tower structure seem very likely. The restoration of the central and transept nave sills was facilitated by the unexpected discovery of well-preserved fragments of the starter and cornice stones of the arched frieze on the west gable, as well as by the excavation of several different motifs from the arched inlays embedded in the vault rubble. The reconstruction of the entire roof structure was presented so clearly that the present form of the church's roof structure can be considered completely identical to its earlier form, especially since the finds also provided numerous clues regarding the details of the crossing tower. Furthermore, a close resemblance to the Romanesque buildings of Lower Franconia has been observed. The cleaning and restoration of the interior, especially the pillars, capitals and vault ribs, and indeed all the stonework, was an extremely laborious and time-consuming task, as several coats of paint (including oil paint) were superimposed and had virtually grown into the porous stone material, so that a complete overhaul by the stonemason and striking of the surfaces with a stock hammer proved necessary. During the entire restoration, nothing was added except for the gallery in the west of the nave, which was essential for the organ installation. The principle was strictly adhered to: to expose or supplement what was already there and to reconstruct what was missing. Even with regard to the painting, which has suffered greatly as a result of the dampness left over from earlier times and is to be restored in a more durable manner in the near future, the work was limited to the simplest surface decoration in order to better emphasize the architectural elements in their dignified simplicity. The restoration work began in 1877 and was completed in 1878. From the above report it emerges that all components located above the main cornice (gable, roof and crossing tower) are to be considered as completely renewed, while all those located below it (in particular the vaults) are to be considered as old and only partially restored. The building records of the General State Archives, which, as mentioned, only begin in 1663, unfortunately do not provide any evidence for the above-mentioned evidence of the former existence of a bell tower above the crossing. However, they do allow the conclusion that the bell tower above the crossing had already been destroyed, or at least disused, long before the Great War. In its place, a bell cage was erected above the southern vault of the transept, as can be seen from the following entry in the building records: 1664 May 16. The bell cage, on which two heavy bells hang, and its sleepers, stock and bow (?), and other supporting structures, are all incredibly old, partly rotten and completely bare, so damaged that ringing poses a great danger to the bells, the vault on which the bells stand, and to the people in the church, including the bell ringer. The addition: "everything is immemorial," suggests that the destruction of the church, to which the entire upper part, including the crossing tower, fell victim, must have occurred during the Peasants' War (or even earlier, during the two sieges of Boxberg in 1470 and 1533), and in any case long before the Thirty Years' War. A second reference is even clearer: May 9 and July 9, 1784. According to expert investigations, that part of the vault above which the bell cage has stood since time immemorial, and beneath which a gallery church, and the main wall upon which the vault rests, are in danger of collapsing. The aforementioned "gallery church," as another reference shows, was located in the southern part of the transept; Further reports from 1794 and 1800 confirm this, proving that it is the bell tower that was still in the same location at the beginning of the restoration in 1877 (see above, p. 227). To accommodate it, the walls of the southern transept ("the main wall") were raised higher, and a massive roof with sound holes was added above it. Otherwise, little can be gleaned from the aforementioned construction records about the church's former appearance. They mainly concern the most necessary repairs, which were carried out with the greatest economy. The following excerpts, for example, demonstrate how barbaric the work was, and which, like the previous ones, we owe to Professor Ehrenberger: 1663 March 10. The church has 21 windows in total, five of which are 6' high, 16 of which are 10' high and 3' wide, plus two large rose windows, one 10' round and in the choir. The rose windows and five windows are completely without glass, and the remaining glass is badly damaged, all destroyed during the dreadful war. Snow and rain fall on the pulpit (through the side skylights). Estimated value: 44 fl. 1663 April 25. Since the above expenditure is too much, it is proposed to brick up 2 of the 11 larger windows and 4 of the smaller ones. In 1784, it was ordered that the damaged vault beneath the bell tower be removed and replaced with timbers. The pastor and congregation prevented the work, which had already begun, because it "would have disfigured the church." In 1666, a large portion of the floor lacked any covering, so that it "looked quite rude and mocking because of the bare earth on which one walked." Repeated roof repairs and, in particular, the reconstruction of damaged or collapsed sections of the churchyard wall are recorded. The latter probably involved the northern retaining wall, which was intended to protect the cemetery surrounding the church and the church itself from the inflow of earth from above. It disappeared in 1794, causing great damage to the relevant parts of the building (see the above report). Unfortunately, the building records tell us nothing about the buildings belonging to the Knights Hospitaller belonging to the church, except for one mention that the stones from an old cellar located behind the church – probably the former order's house – were to be used to repair the churchyard wall (August 6, 1691). (The term "cloister" in a contract dated February 8, 1731, refers, as is clear from the context, to the central section of the nave and transept, forming a cross.) Building description. The church is a Romanesque, three-aisled, cross-shaped pillar basilica with a semicircular apse and two side apses, vaulted in a tied system (see floor plan Fig. 67). The dimensions are not large, but the proportions are so fortunate that the building appears larger than it is. The whole thing must have been erected quickly according to a uniform plan; only in one place can a deliberate deviation from the original layout be detected. After the first bay of the nave – construction began in the east as usual – was completed, it seems that people came to the conclusion that the strongly projecting pillars of the side aisles unnecessarily narrowed them and that the side walls were sufficiently strong to support the small vaults. At the same time, the distance between the cumbersome arcade pillars was reduced from 1.66 to 1.86 m. 1.35 m to 2.00 m, thus giving the western part of the nave a freer, more airy character (see Fig. 68). The main apse, like the side apses, is vaulted with a semi-dome. In all three, at the front corners, at moderate intervals below the impost, which is accentuated by a cornice, there is a flat cuboid with a straight, simply decorated front. It projects slightly like a console, allowing a slight narrowing of the semicircle in the upper parts. This arrangement has never been encountered by the author before, and the purpose of which is unclear, since, given the existing dimensions, such a small saving in span would not have been possible, even for the large semi-dome, let alone for the side apses. The seven square cross vaults that cover the choir, transept, and nave are of identical construction, although they have the same width (an average of 5 meters). Broad, unarticulated, heavy-duty transverse arches separate the vaults, whose ribs appear simple with a sturdy pear-shaped rib, and only in the chancel are they somewhat more richly profiled, with a bulge and pear-shaped rib. The ribs of the southern transept vault show a remarkable deviation: the edges of the square stones, projecting far in front of the coping, are chamfered and set with hemispheres on the slope, an original but somewhat heavy-duty motif. [The above-mentioned bell cage stood above this until 1877]. The keystones show simple arched sections between the ribs and flat-pattern decoration, and are circularly hollowed in the center. While the transverse arches of the nave are supported by the capitals of the half-columns, the diagonal ribs emanate from consoles that are joined to the column capitals and covered by a common abacus. Some of them have a piece of column shaft, decorated with grotesques or similar motifs on the underside (see Fig. 69). In the choir and transept, however, the diagonals of round columns also rise in the corners. There are no special shield arches anywhere; instead, the capping line, i.e., the shield arch line (incorrectly depicted as a semicircle in our sections), which forms a steep basket arch at a significant rise in the apex, lies directly against the surface of the shield wall. Otherwise, the pointed arch form prevails everywhere, both in the transverse and diagonal arches, as well as in the arcade arches. The cover plate of the half-column capital and the consoles extends as a transom cornice around the entire "cloister" (see above). A second, strong horizontal emphasis is formed by the transom cornice of the arcade arches, which curves around the half-column supports. The clumsy arcade pillars stand on a richly structured base consisting of cornice, round bar, plate, slope and foot, while the base cornice running all the way around the walls has only a round bar and foot plate. In contrast to the somewhat cumbersome ribbed cross vaults of the "cloister," the vaults of the side aisles—two of which, in keeping with the tied system, are arranged for each central bay—are spanned without ribs on corner consoles between heavy, unprofiled transverse arches. The latter, too, are supported only in the first two bays (see above), and in the rest by simply decorated corbels. In the southeast corner (at the transept) and northwest corner (at the west front), corner columns are exceptionally installed, consistent in both aisles. The passage from the side aisle to the transept has undergone a peculiar narrowing on both sides, as a second pillar with an arch has been inserted within the opening corresponding to the transverse arch. At the end of the north aisle, a spiral staircase cut out of the strong front wall leads to the church floor. The windows, like the doors (see below), are all round-arched and smoothly cut into the walls, without rods or the like at the corners and with only a moderate slope. In the transept, the aforementioned impost cornice runs to a dead end on both sides of the upper windows; in the nave, this disadvantage was easily avoided by setting the windows accordingly higher (see Fig. 68). The round windows in the gables are particularly attractive. The one above the apse appears to be framed by a strong "Norman" zigzag and has a panel pierced all around by circular cutouts. Ornamental decoration is used with extreme sparingness in the interior; except for the capitals and consoles, and to a limited extent on the keystones, there are no ornaments to be found anywhere. The forms generally adhere to the Romanesque canon, but in some places, attempts at bulbous forms and a freer, more natural treatment of the foliage and tendrils are already apparent. The transitional period is thus revealed not only in the vaulting (pointed arches), but also in the intrusion of Gothic forms. The interior is of great beauty and will be significantly enhanced once the planned painting (see above) is completed and the uniform, cold tone of the stone has disappeared. Despite all the compactness and coarseness, which is particularly evident in the arcades and vaulting, and despite all the poor ornamentation, the eye still wanders with pleasure through the high nave and the bright transept to the choir, where the colorfully glazed round window above the concha illuminates effectively. In terms of clarity, clarity, and uniformity of its interior, the St. John's Church in Wölching undoubtedly ranks first among the oldest churches in Franconia and Swabia (see collotype plate XIX). Of the details inside, it is worth mentioning: above the sacrament niche in the choir there is a completely mutilated relief of the Crucifixion, which, judging by the shape of the letters, dates back to the 14th century. The adjacent door leads outside. The sacristy may once have been located in this corner, as usual, and is mentioned repeatedly in the building records of the General State Archives, but without further details. A now bricked-up door located at the top (about 4 meters above the floor) in the west wall of the northern transept probably provided access from outside to a gallery of the Knights of the Order and may have been directly connected to the hospital above. Beneath half the choir and the apse is a low crypt, accessible via a narrow staircase through an opening in the floor. Its shape is circular, covered by a circular vault supported by a central pillar (see Fig. 71). Four slanted slit windows provide the small space with minimal illumination. Of particular interest is the octagonal capital of the central column (see Fig. 72), from which eight ribs extend and gradually taper into the round barrel vault. That the unusual circular shape of the crypt in this case, as so often, is connected with the general idea of ​​the circular structure of the Holy Sepulchre (cf. Dehio and Bezold, die kirchliche Baukunst des Abendlandes, Vol. I, Stuttgart 1892, pp. 35 ff., 542 and 554 ff.), seems just as irrefutable as the assumption that the Knights Hospitaller Commander would have had their tomb here. The exterior of the church reflects the interior: uniform, simple, yet beautiful and stately. The restoration work, carried out with great piety, is noticeable only in the currently somewhat lighter color of the material used. The walls, constructed of rubble stone, are unstructured and decorated only with simple but robust main and base cornices. The latter runs horizontally around the entire building, regardless of the variation in the floor level. In contrast to the interior, the exterior is still dominated exclusively by round arches. The windows also appear without frames or moldings, with the exception of the apse windows, which have robust round-bar frames. Apart from the southern side portal, only the three apses, the west facade, and the gables are somewhat more richly decorated. Actually, however, it is only a round-arch frieze here, which has a stimulating effect and displays the same decoration by means of volute-like insets or underlays as in the apse of the Bronnbach monastery church (see Section I, Plate I). Here, the stonemason had a great opportunity to explore his wealth of forms and ideas, to demonstrate his imagination in diverse ornamentation and figurative grotesque creatures. (The motifs of the above-mentioned finds have been very skillfully used in the restored sections.) The gable ends also appear to be decorated in part with grotesques and squatting figures, the cover plates with a round-arch pattern and diagonal cut (see Fig. 73). In keeping with the overall simplicity, the main portal and south portal (both completely intact) are richly structured, yet treated with extreme restraint in ornamentation and a complete renunciation of figurative decoration. The south portal on the front side of the church (see collotype XX) can be described as a classic example of noble and simple design. Particularly attractive is a bas-relief of triangular tendrils above the apex of the arch, below an equal-armed cross crowning the gable. To achieve a colorful effect, the round columns in the jamb of the main portal were made of red sandstone, and the polished limestone cylinder on the south portal was painted red in a similar manner, as the existing paint remains demonstrate. Traces of paint are also visible elsewhere, on the tympanum stone, capitals, and bases. The front facade was provided with a (wooden?) vestibule in the usual manner. The traces of the pilasters are still clearly visible in places. The asymmetrical arrangement of the pilasters bordering the nave on the main facade is very odd. The left-hand projection is about 0.30 m closer to the main portal than the right-hand one, so that a corresponding projection to the left had to be made above the projection line of the northern aisle roof in order to reach the corner of the rising nave at the top. That this was the correction of an oversight when marking out the left half is obvious. Otherwise, the right-hand pillar projection would not have been moved away from the ashlar edge of the portal by the specified width from below, thus avoiding the unsightly ledge that resulted. The presence of the aforementioned spiral staircase on the left side inside the wall has nothing to do with this. On the rear, it can be described as faulty, or at least as odd, that the tip of the semi-conical roof of the main apse projects freely in front of the wall into the curve of the window above. Furthermore, the technical aspects of the exterior have also been treated with the utmost care. The modern, eight-sided crossing tower contributes significantly to the overall impression and effectively enlivens the silhouette. Dating the Wölching church to within one or two decades seems difficult. If one were to place the construction of the church, which was apparently erected in rapid succession, in the 13th century, then, given the clumsiness and uncertainty evident in both the Gothic forms and the construction, the year 1210 would be considered the upper limit. However, following Bronnbach's analogy, it is equally conceivable that the church had already been completed by the turn of the 12th century. The overall impression is certainly still thoroughly Romanesque. The church is rich in tombs, which changed their location during the last restoration, and partly even before (cf. Schönhuth, op. cit., p. 33 ff.) and are now located in the following places: I. Inside. a. In the south transept: In the gable wall, two niches (arcosolia) are arranged side by side, vaulted with shallow arches. Each niche contains a Romanesque cover plate above the empty (?) coffin space. One contains, in low relief, the image of a man reclining with folded hands, his upper body exposed and his lower body covered only by a hairy (?) garment belted around his waist. Bare feet protrude from beneath. The face has been cut off. Romanesque tendrils run all around the horizontal and beveled parts of the rim (see Fig. 74). The second stone shows only a sword grasped by a hand, and above it a crudely carved human mask or flat head in low relief. The ornament here runs only along the upper part of the rim (see Fig. 75). The absence of any inscription is doubly regrettable in this case, since our two monuments, along with that of Notburga in Hochhausen am Neckar, are undoubtedly the oldest monuments of this type in the Neckar and Tauber region. Their forms are so ancient that one would involuntarily place them a century before the construction of the church. As can be seen from a contract dated February 8, 1731, in the building records, the gravestones in the choir were moved at that time. These two slabs are unlikely to have been included at that time, since the method of burial in wall niches (arcosolia), in the early Christian style, makes a decidedly older impression. b.
